message.content: The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large – on the order of 10^43.  This estimate comes from the Shannon number, which was derived by Claude Shannon in 1950 as a lower bound for the game‑tree complexity of chess.  While the exact count is still unknown (the search space is too huge to enumerate exhaustively), the consensus among researchers is that there are roughly 10^43 to 10^45 distinct positions that satisfy all of the rules of chess.
